questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Repeal of the earlier territorial restriction
questions.learningObjective: Explain what repealing the 1820 territorial restriction did and did not change
questions.stem: In a planning file, the note on the old line records that the 1820 restriction no longer has force. Explain what the repeal settled and what it left alone.

answer.exemplar: Repealing the Missouri restriction removed the federal bar on slavery north of 36 degrees 30 minutes in the Louisiana Purchase and left the question of slavery in the territories to the settlers themselves. It changed no state already in the Union, freed no enslaved person, and gave Congress no new power to restrict slavery; it only renounced the power the government had once claimed.

questions.explanation: Repeal took the question away from Congress and gave it to the territory, but it freed no one and altered no state. The change concerned the status of future territories, nothing else.
questions.hint: Ask what changes and what stays as it was.

answer.exemplar: Popular sovereignty moved the decision on slavery in a territory from Congress to the settlers, on the theory that the people living on the land were the proper judges of what suited it. questions.topic: What the debates of 1858 revealed
questions.learningObjective: Explain the northern position the debates established
questions.stem: An Illinois campaign memo on the debates asks what the northern party was arguing for. Explain the position the debates set out and left aside.

answer.exemplar: In Illinois the Republicans did not argue that the Constitution made slavery illegal everywhere; they argued that it was a moral wrong and that Congress had no power to spread it, and they pressed the point that the Missouri restriction had been unconstitutional in 1820. The debates thus fixed a northern position of opposition to the extension of slavery while leaving the question of abolition inside the existing states untouched.

questions.explanation: The northern position was against expansion, not abolition, and the debates sharpened it into a constitutional argument as well as a moral one. That is the platform the party carried into 1860.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how the 1850 act shifted the burden of proof in fugitive cases
questions.stem: A planner's memo on an old courthouse annex asks what the 1850 law did to the burden of proof. Explain the change it made.

answer.exemplar: The act placed the burden squarely on the person claimed as a fugitive, since a slaveholder's sworn statement was enough to justify certification and removal without a jury. Evidence of a free birth, of a manumission, or of long residence in a free state was hard to present before a single commissioner, so the law made freedom far harder to prove than slavery was to claim.

questions.explanation: A single sworn claim carried the burden, and no jury weighed the evidence. That is why the law made capture easy and defence nearly impossible.
questions.hint: Ask who had to prove what.

options.misconception: Believes a trial preceded certification

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Repeal of the earlier territorial restriction
questions.learningObjective: Explain how repeal changed the allocation of power over slavery in territories
questions.stem: A territory school memo on a new school lot explains who would now decide the slavery question in a territory. Explain what the repeal did to congressional power.

answer.exemplar: Repealing the Missouri restriction did not enlarge the federal power to restrict slavery; it renounced the claim to that power and handed the decision to the settlers of each territory. The practical result was that Congress could no longer bar slavery in the territories and could do nothing to prevent it either, since the choice belonged to the local electorate under popular sovereignty.

questions.explanation: Repeal took the question away from Congress and gave it to the territory. Congress neither kept a veto nor gained a power to act, and that is the whole of the bargain popular sovereignty struck.
questions.hint: Ask who was left holding the decision.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Repeal of the earlier territorial restriction
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish what the 1850 settlement did from what the 1854 act did
questions.stem: A zoning file note on the old line explains what happened to the 1820 rule on paper. Explain the difference between the action of 1850 and the action of 1854.

answer.exemplar: The 1850 settlement repealed the Missouri restriction for the remainder of the Louisiana Purchase and organised the newly acquired Mexican cession territories with popular sovereignty. The 1854 act went further, carrying popular sovereignty into Kansas and Nebraska and striking the 1820 restriction wherever it still stood, so that by 1854 the compromise of 1820 no longer governed the question of slavery in any territory of the United States.

questions.explanation: The two steps are often confused: 1850 repealed the restriction and applied popular sovereignty to the new lands, while 1854 extended popular sovereignty and finished the 1820 rule. Together they ended the line as a governing force.
questions.hint: Ask what each year did with the rule.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A legislature that changed the voting rules
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the true claims about the Kansas election and the state constitution
questions.stem: A compiler's note on the Kansas courthouse states four claims: one, Missouri residents crossed into Kansas for the 1855 territorial election and used stuffed ballot boxes; two, the Lecompton constitution was rejected by Kansas voters in separate referendums in 1858 and 1859; three, the 1855 legislature wrote a state constitution and sent it to Congress without any popular vote; four, Kansas was admitted to the Union in 1857 under a constitution drawn up before the territory was settled. Which two claims are accurate?

options.text: Statements one and two are accurate, while three and four are not
Statements one and three are accurate, while two and four are not
options.misconception: Believes the 1855 body drafted a constitution alone

options.text: Statements two and four are accurate, while one and three are not
options.misconception: Believes Kansas entered the Union in 1857

options.text: Statements three and four are accurate, while one and two are not
options.misconception: Believes the Lecompton constitution was ratified

questions.explanation: The border fraud of 1855 and the rejection of the Lecompton constitution are the accurate claims. The 1855 body did not write a constitution on its own, and Kansas entered the Union in 1861 under the Topeka document.
questions.hint: Ask when Kansas actually entered the Union.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The citizenship holding in the 1857 decision
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how the ruling changed the categories of people in federal law
questions.stem: A citizenship file memo on the courthouse asks what the 1857 decision did to the categories of people the country used. Which assessment is best?

options.text: It merged free and enslaved Black people into one class barred from citizenship
It separated free people from enslaved ones and protected the free
options.misconception: Believes the ruling protected free people

options.text: It left the categories untouched and changed only federal procedure
options.misconception: Believes the change was procedural

options.text: It created a new category of protected persons for the northern states
options.misconception: Invents a new legal category

questions.explanation: The opinion spoke of a race whose ancestors were imported as slaves and treated free and enslaved people alike, erasing the distinction on which northern claims to citizenship rested. That merger is why the ruling was read as far-reaching.
questions.hint: Ask how many categories the opinion used.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Effect of the 1857 decision on the political calendar
questions.learningObjective: Identify the politician hurt by the timing of the 1857 ruling
questions.stem: A presidency file memo on the 1857 event asks who suffered politically from the ruling's timing. Which answer fits?

options.text: President Buchanan, who had pressed the Court and then claimed the credit
The northern Republicans, who had campaigned against the decision
options.misconception: Blames the Republicans for the timing

options.text: Chief Justice Taney, whose reputation the ruling destroyed
options.misconception: Blames Taney for the timing

options.text: The southern senators, who had asked the Court to decide the matter
options.misconception: Blames the southern senators

questions.explanation: Buchanan pressed the Court to settle the question and then claimed the settlement as his own, so the decision's timing cut against him. It also discredited the popular sovereignty his party had relied on.
questions.hint: Ask who had asked the Court to rule.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the election of 1860 produced a crisis
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the winning platform was read as a threat in the south

stimulus.body: A public meeting file on the courthouse steps records a former member of Congress telling the crowd that the election just won was the work of the people he had fought for forty years, and that he would be the sworn enemy of the rights of those same people. The night clerk notes that no newspaper in the town printed the speech the following week.

questions.stem: A public meeting file on the platform pledges asks what made the result a crisis. Which explanation fits the evidence?

options.text: The winning party campaigned to restrict slavery's expansion, so the south read a mandate against it
The election was decided by the House of Representatives, so nobody had a mandate
options.misconception: Confuses the count with 1824

options.text: The winning party had pledged immediate abolition throughout the south
options.misconception: Invents an abolition pledge

options.text: The losing side won the popular vote, so a recount was constitutionally required
options.misconception: Invents a recount requirement

questions.explanation: The Republican platform of 1860 held that slavery must not be extended, and southern leaders read a win with no southern votes as a mandate to act against them. The reaction came before the new administration could take office.
questions.hint: Ask what the winning party said about expansion.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the debates of 1858 revealed
questions.learningObjective: Explain the constitutional argument advanced in the 1858 debates
questions.stem: A north position file on the debates asks what argument the challenger's side advanced. Explain the case it made and the limits it accepted.

answer.exemplar: The northern argument in Illinois was that slavery was a moral wrong and that Congress had no constitutional power to extend it, so that the Missouri restriction of 1820 had been ineffective from the start. The side accepted that question as settled inside the states already in the Union, so its demand was confined to stopping the spread of the institution and leaving abolition to those states, which is precisely what the party platform of 1860 repeated.

questions.explanation: The northern position was anti-expansion rather than abolition, and it was argued in constitutional as well as moral terms. The debates set that limit clearly, and the party platform of 1860 repeated it.
questions.hint: Ask what the northern party did not demand.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Mechanics of the fugitive slave law
questions.learningObjective: Identify the evidential rules the 1850 act imposed on a claim
questions.stem: A reach file memorandum on the 1850 act states four claims: one, a claimant's sworn statement was enough to justify a certificate of removal; two, the person claimed could not testify before the commissioner; three, the commissioner was required to hold a hearing at which both sides called witnesses; four, the act applied only to people claimed in a slaveholding state. Which two claims are accurate?

options.text: Statements one and two are accurate, while three and four are not
Statements one and three are accurate, while two and four are not
options.misconception: Believes a hearing with witnesses was required

options.text: Statements two and four are accurate, while one and three are not
options.misconception: Believes the act was limited to slave states

options.text: Statements three and four are accurate, while one and two are not
options.misconception: Believes the accused could testify freely

questions.explanation: A sworn claim and a commissioner's certificate were enough, and the person named could not testify, so no hearing on the facts took place. The machinery was one-sided from the start.
questions.hint: Ask whose testimony the process would not hear.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: Repeal of the earlier territorial restriction
questions.learningObjective: Sequence how a rule on paper ran into a rigged count
questions.stem: A sequence file memo on the territorial question lists four steps: one, the 1850 arrangement leaves the new territories' status to the settlers; two, the 1854 act extends that rule to Kansas and Nebraska; three, settlers of opposing views move in, and the 1855 election is decided by voters from Missouri; four, the question of who lawfully governs Kansas is still unresolved when the 1857 ruling is handed down. Which ordering is correct?

options.text: The 1850 arrangement, the 1854 extension, the rigged election, then the ruling
The 1854 extension, the 1850 arrangement, the ruling, then the rigged election
options.misconception: Reverses the first two steps in time

options.text: The rigged election, the 1850 arrangement, the 1854 extension, then the ruling
options.misconception: Starts with the count rather than the rule

options.text: The ruling, the 1850 arrangement, the 1854 extension, then the rigged election
options.misconception: Runs the sequence backwards

questions.explanation: The rule came in 1850, was extended in 1854, met a rigged election in 1855 and was still contested when the Court spoke in 1857. The Court answered a constitutional question and left the Kansas one untouched.
questions.hint: Ask which step came first in time.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: A legislature that changed the voting rules
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how control of voting rules shaped the Kansas territorial result

stimulus.body: Notice to the inhabitants of the county: the polls for the election of a delegate to the territorial legislature will be opened at the courthouse on the day appointed, and the oaths required by law will be administered to such persons as shall claim a right to vote. The commissioners will be guided by the law and by the returns of the supervisors, and no person shall be molested for going to the polls to exercise the rights guaranteed to him.

questions.stem: A file note on the notice quotes the proclamation. What does it reveal about the voting rules the legislature controlled?

options.text: The legislature shaped who could vote and how the count was made at the polls
The legislature set the rules but county officials had no discretion of their own
options.misconception: Believes no local discretion existed

options.text: The notice shows voting was left to the settlers with no official role at all
options.misconception: Thinks there was no official role

options.text: The notice shows the polls were open to every resident without any qualification
options.misconception: Believes universal suffrage was in force

questions.explanation: Oaths, appointments and the handling of the count were in the hands of officials the territorial majority controlled, so the rules were the real battleground. Kansas proved the point when boxes were broken and tallies replaced.
questions.hint: Ask who administered the oaths and the count.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.topic: The citizenship holding in the 1857 decision
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the 1857 ruling left to the states to decide

stimulus.body: A clerk's file memo on the courthouse annex records that the state legislature had resolved that persons of African descent were not citizens of the state, and had instructed the county clerk to strike their names from the jury rolls and from the lists of qualified voters at the polls. The clerk asks whether the decision of 1857 requires the state to take any further step, or whether it merely permitted what the legislature has already done.

questions.stem: A clerk's file memo on the jury roll asks what the 1857 decision left to the states. Which answer is correct?

options.text: The legal status of Black residents within each state, which several states then tightened
The number of federal judges in each district, which the Court then fixed
options.misconception: Misreads what was left to the states

options.text: The wording of the state constitutions on slavery, which the Court rewrote
options.misconception: Claims the Court rewrote constitutions

options.text: The dates of the presidential elections, which the Court reset
options.misconception: Claims the Court changed elections

questions.explanation: The Court settled the national question and pushed the personal one into state law, and states used that opening to narrow rights further. The decision thus multiplied local exclusions rather than settling them.
questions.hint: Ask what the memo says the states were left to decide.
